articles.title: Improving crowdsourcing for AI through cognitive-inspired data engineering
articles.authors: Gunnar P. Epping, Andrew Caplin, Erik Duhaime, William R. Holmes, Daniel Martin, Jennifer S. Trueblood
articles.abstract: Crowdsourcing offers a fast and cost-efficient approach to obtaining human-labeled datasets. However, crowdsourced datasets and the models trained on them can inherit the cognitive constraints and biases of their annotators. In a process we refer to as cognitive-inspired data engineering, we investigate whether ideas from cognitive science can be applied to mitigate the presence of cognitive constraints and cognitive biases in crowdsourced datasets and, as a result, improve the performance of models trained on these datasets. We evaluate our approach by crowdsourcing labels for medical image diagnostic tasks using two different crowdsourcing platforms across two experiments. In Experiment 1, we collect subjective probability judgments from novice annotators through Amazon Mechanical Turk and, in Experiment 2, we collect subjective probability judgments and binary classifications from skilled annotators through DiagnosUs, a crowdsourcing platform specializing in medical and scientific data annotation. In both experiments, we find that recalibrating subjective probability judgments reduces bias, yielding more accurate crowdsourced datasets and more accurate models trained on them. Our results suggest that cognitive-inspired data engineering offers a promising avenue to improve the quality of crowdsourced datasets, with consistent downstream benefits for machine learning models.

articles.title: How accurate are Bayes factor-based null hypothesis tests? A simulation study
articles.authors: Daniel J. Schad, Martin Modrák
articles.abstract: Bayes factor null hypothesis tests provide a viable alternative to frequentist measures of evidence quantification. Bayes factors for realistic data sets in areas like psychology cannot be calculated exactly and require numerical approximations to complex integrals. Crucially, the accuracy of these approximations, i.e., whether an approximate Bayes factor corresponds to the exact Bayes factor, is unknown, and may depend on data, prior, and likelihood. We recently developed a novel statistical procedure, marginal simulation-based calibration (SBC) for Bayes factors, to test whether computed Bayes factors for a given analysis are accurate. Here, we use marginal SBC for Bayes factors and calibration plots to test whether Bayes factors are calculated accurately for some common cognitive designs. We use the bridgesampling/brms packages in R. We run analyses for three commonly used designs in psychology and psycholinguistics: (a) a design with random effects for subjects only, (b) a Latin square design with crossed random effects for subjects and items, but a single fixed factor, and (c) a Latin square 2x2 design with crossed random effects for subjects and items. We find that Bayes factor estimates turn out accurate in cases when the bridgesampling algorithm does not issue a warning message, but can be biased and variable when a warning message is shown. These results support the use of brms/bridgesampling for null hypothesis Bayes factor tests in commonly used factorial designs. They also suggest that when a warning message is issued, Bayes factor results should not be trusted. The results show that it is practical to check whether Bayes factors are computed correctly.

articles.title: Reject common measures like d′ and Corrected Recognition, embrace da: Simulation explorations of single- and multi-point recognition measures of sensitivity
articles.authors: Adva Levi, Raz Danino, Caren M. Rotello, Yonatan Goshen-Gottstein
articles.abstract: In this article, we address the high prevalence of false discoveries in recognition memory research. Using Monte Carlo simulations, our goal was to find a valid measure of performance that reliably separates the contribution of sensitivity (accuracy) from that of bias . Relevant to myriad tasks, most notably old–new recognition memory, the simulations revealed that common measures confound sensitivity with bias, a finding termed the “measurement crisis.” As a solution, we propose a version of d-sub-a ( d a ). We ran comprehensive simulations to evaluate the validity of sensitivity measures, including P r = HR − FAR, A ′, d ′, and AUC g , in addition to d a . Memory “signals” were randomly sampled from lure and target distributions. Sensitivity measures generated from iso-sensitive conditions that differed in bias were compared using t -tests, across thousands of simulations. For bias-independent measures, the rate of significant results should be 5%. We manipulated several parameters, including the form of the distributions (i.e., from three prominent models of recognition–memory: unequal variance signal detection [UVSD], double-high threshold [2HT], dual-process signal detection [DPSD]), the distance between their means, their relative variance, the placement of response criteria, the sample size, and the number of simulated trials. Results demonstrated that under most experimental scenarios, only d a was unaffected by changes in bias. In contrast, all common measures typically exhibited alarmingly high false discovery rates, exceeding 5%. The rates rose to 100% with larger sample sizes and a large number of trials. These findings indicate that d a warrants serious consideration as the default measure of sensitivity.

articles.title: Ensemble clustering: A practical tutorial
articles.authors: Caroline X. Gao, Shengqi Wang, Ye Zhu, Myriam Ziou, Shu Mei Teo, Catherine L. Smith, Derek Chiu, Aline Talhouk, Mengmeng Wang, Wenhua Yu, Sue M. Cotton, Dominic Dwyer
articles.abstract: Cluster analysis is an explorative analytical method, serving as a critical tool in psychology, psychiatry, and related fields to map heterogeneous data into meaningful subgroups. Despite their extensive historical use, traditional clustering techniques suffer from a lack of stability, robustness, and generalisability. These issues stem from the inherent difficulties of the clustering optimisation problem as well as the stochastic nature of algorithm optimisers. To address these challenges, we demonstrate the use of methods utilising ensemble learning techniques to combine clustering results from different algorithms, model specifications, and/or sampled sub-datasets to form a single, more reliable consensus of clustering solutions. We detail ensemble clustering principles and variations in base clustering generation models and ensemble methods. More importantly, detailed introductions in existing R libraries and practical examples using R code are provided to guide users in both implementing and optimising ensemble clustering models. As a practical tutorial, we then include simulation studies of real-world data to demonstrate the substantial benefit of ensemble clustering compared with single-run clustering models. The resources presented here will enable researchers to apply advanced clustering techniques to decompose heterogeneous and complex psychological data into stable subgroups.

articles.title: Time after time, the best–worst scaling method is more reliable than ranking
articles.authors: Garston Liang, Mackenzie Glover, Guy E. Hawkins
articles.abstract: Two popular methods of preference elicitation are rankings and best–worst scaling (BWS). Rankings, while simple and widely adopted, can be burdensome with larger item sets and fail to capture indifference between options that are neither loved nor hated. Best–worst scaling is a survey method that sidesteps the set size problem by capitalizing on people’s natural capacity to identify preferences at the extremes. Across three experiments, our primary finding is that elicited preferences for ranking and BWS methods align, and that BWS methods provide additional resolution to resolve the indifference between middling options where rankings can struggle as well as the relative importance of each option. Moreover, we show that BWS methods exhibit greater test–retest reliability compared to rankings, even over time frames as short as minutes. Taken together, our results privilege BWS as a reliable and readily accessible alternative to ranking methods for preference elicitation.

articles.title: Subjective age of acquisition norms for 30,849 Russian words
articles.authors: Andrei A. Grigoriev, Konstantin V. Sugonyaev, Svetlana A. Pashneva, Ekaterina A. Valueva, Nikolai A. Grigorev
articles.abstract: Age of acquisition (AoA) is a key psycholinguistic variable known to influence lexical and conceptual processing across a broad range of tasks. However, existing Russian datasets are small and mainly limited to picturable nouns and verbs. In this study, we collected AoA ratings for 30,849 Russian words that represent a broad vocabulary range. Ratings were collected from 2,201 adult respondents in both in-person and online sessions. Reliability assessed via bootstrap split-half correlations was high (mean r = 0.895, 95% CI [.893, .897]). To validate the subjective AoA estimates, we administered vocabulary tests to school students from grades 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10. Two validation procedures were used: grade-level validation and within-grade validation. The former related the grade level at which an item was reliably known with the adult ratings, the latter related adult AoA to students’ accuracy. Subjective AoA strongly predicted objective AoA measures ( r = 0.805) and showed consistent negative relations with student accuracy across grades. Correlations with existing Russian AoA datasets ( r = 0.68–0.91) further supported the reliability of the norms. The new ratings also showed expected correlations with word frequency, length, concreteness, imageability, and familiarity. The resulting norms provide the largest and most comprehensive AoA resource for the Russian language and can support future research in psycholinguistics, lexical processing, and language development. All norms are publicly available on OSF.

articles.title: The Honor of a Leader: Examining the Content of Honor-Congruent Leadership Prototypes
articles.authors: Aaron L. Pomerantz, Ryan P. Brown
articles.abstract: Across three studies, we investigated how honor norms are associated with leadership prototypes. An archival, national-level study and an individual-level correlational study both linked honor norms to tough, reputation-conscious leadership and preferences for male leaders. A pre-registered quasi-experiment refined our understanding of these associations. Participants “designed” an ideal leader in either the presence or absence of intergroup conflict and results again showed that honor endorsement predicted preferences for certain leader characteristics (e.g., tough, protective) and for male leaders. High intergroup conflict increased both preferences across all participants, regardless of their level of honor endorsement, and the main effects of both honor and conflict on male leader favorability ratings were partially mediated by preferences for honor-congruent leader characteristics. Together, these studies suggest that honor functions as a cultural logic that informs leadership prototypes, shaping collective perceptions of idealized power and influence.

articles.title: Storytelling as a Bridge: Examining the Psychological Processes of Fictional Writing on Intergroup Understanding
articles.authors: Xun Zhu
articles.abstract: Reading a positive story about an outgroup reduces prejudice, but can writing a story about the outgroup have similar effects? Three experiments examined whether and how writing a fictional story about an outgroup character can improve writers’ perceptions of the outgroup. Study 1 ( N = 727) showed that narrative writing increased warmth and competence perceptions of the character, regardless of whether writers described cooperating directly with the character, as characters themselves, to complete a positive task or wrote the story from the character’s perspective. Higher perceived warmth, but not competence, was associated with lower intergroup anxiety and stronger empathy toward the outgroup, which in turn predicted perceived dangerousness. Two follow-up experiments sought to replicate these findings using a different character (Study 2; N = 287) and a comparison with nonnarrative persuasive writing (Study 3; N = 343). The findings contribute to theories addressing the intersection of intergroup contact, creative writing, and narrative communication.

articles.title: From “Them” to “Us”: Intergroup Contact Leads to Improved Intergroup Attitudes through Building Common Ingroup Identity: Longitudinal Evidence from Four European Countries
articles.authors: Joanna Lindström, Siddartha Aradhya, Sabina Čehajić-Clancy
articles.abstract: The successful integration of ethnic minorities is largely contingent on establishing positive relations between minority and majority groups. Drawing on the common ingroup identity model, we argue that for minority youth, intergroup contact (e.g., friendship) with majority youth predicts more positive attitudes toward the majority group because it may foster a stronger common-ingroup identity. Using three-wave panel data from the Children of Immigrants Longitudinal Survey in Four European Countries ( N = 5,447), we found support for our hypothesis: intergroup contact predicted more positive attitudes toward the majority groups over time, due to an increase in common-ingroup identification. Findings suggest that intergroup friendships may play a key role in immigrant youth integration, precisely through facilitating a sense of belonging to a shared identity with the majority group.

articles.title: Can Generative Large Language Models Serve as Raters for Test Development? A Systematic Evaluation Across Tasks, Models, and Inference Configurations
articles.authors: Mina Son, Philseok Lee
articles.abstract: The present study investigates the effectiveness of generative large language models (LLMs) as raters across three common rating tasks: (a) social desirability ratings, (b) content validity ratings, and (c) trait importance ratings. Specifically, we examine reliability and validity of LLM-generated ratings across varying occupational contexts, rating methods, LLM families (i.e., GPT-4, GPT-5, and Sonnet 4.5), and inference configurations (i.e., prompt design and temperature settings). Results indicate that LLM ratings exhibit strong reliability and convergent validity in social desirability ratings across occupational contexts, as well as acceptable convergence with human ratings in Likert-type content validity evaluations. In contrast, reliability and convergent validity for trait importance ratings were inconsistent across occupational contexts. Variations in prompt design and temperature settings generally produced small to negligible effects on reliability and validity. Overall, the findings suggest that LLMs can function as effective supplementary raters in test development and validation processes, although greater caution is warranted for certain rating tasks. Practical implications and directions for future research are discussed.

articles.title: Whose Sincerely Held Beliefs Count? Political Ideology Shapes Perceptions of Religious Exemption Requests
articles.authors: Mary Katz, Nava Caluori, Michael H. Pasek
articles.abstract: Four studies collectively investigate whether schematic and political biases predict how people conceptualize sincerely held religious beliefs and reason about religious exemptions. Studies 1a ( N = 99) and 1b ( N = 151) suggest that U.S. Americans schematically associate conservative (but not liberal) stances on religion-relevant issues with sincerely held religious belief. Studies 2 and 3 investigate how politically diverse U.S. Americans evaluate exemption requests that are either schema-consistent (conservative request; Study 2; N = 402) or inconsistent (liberal request; Study 3; N = 400) and reveal that people might not exclusively rely on these schemas for judgments about religious exemption requests, as people are more willing to grant exemptions to both conservative schema-consistent and liberal schema-inconsistent religious claims than to nonreligious claims. However, political ideology critically shapes judgments about the religious sincerity of beliefs, whether denying exemption requests constitutes First Amendment violations, and whether exemptions should ultimately be granted.

articles.title: Intergroup Competition Promotes Intragroup Cooperation: A Meta-Analysis of Social Dilemmas
articles.authors: Tycho van Tartwijk, Angelo Romano, Leticia Micheli, Daniel Balliet
articles.abstract: Current theories pose that intergroup competition elevates intragroup cooperation and put forward hypotheses about conditions that increase the magnitude of this effect. Here, we report a preregistered meta-analysis of studies using experimental games that manipulate the presence of intergroup competition and its effect on intragroup cooperation. Our investigation reveals the overall direction and magnitude of the effect, which addresses mixed empirical findings. We identified 25 articles to meet inclusion criteria, which yielded 70 effect sizes. A multilevel random effects model revealed a medium positive effect of intergroup competition on intragroup cooperation ( g = .677, N = 6,051). Studies involving intergroup competition with interdependence produced a strong effect, whereas this effect was weaker for studies without interdependence. Our findings present meta-analytic evidence that intergroup competition promotes intragroup cooperation and identify opportunities for future research.

articles.title: Why Do We Talk About Race? Examining Goals in Discussions About Race in Interracial Friendships
articles.authors: Ashley L. Berkebile-Weinberg, Jennifer R. Steele
articles.abstract: Shared goals are a pillar of effective intergroup contact, yet little research has examined the specific goals that motivate people to engage in intergroup discussions. Across two studies, we assessed the goals of Latine (Study 1) and Black (Study 2) participants, compared to White (Studies 1 and 2) participants, during race-related discussions with a racial ingroup or outgroup friend. Participants from all three racial groups expressed a greater desire to socially connect with racially minoritized versus White friends. White participants’ goals to learn and express egalitarian values were higher in discussions about race with Latine and Black, versus White, friends. By contrast, White participants expressed a lower desire to challenge their friends and manage their group image relative to Latine and Black participants. Participants’ primary conversation goals were to socially connect and learn; however, White participants’ goals shifted more depending on whether they were speaking to a racial ingroup or outgroup friend.

articles.title: The Impact of Regulatory Goals on the Disclosure of Self-presentational Vulnerabilities
articles.authors: Sohyun Bae, Natalie Truong Faust, Sharon Ng
articles.abstract: Individuals often disclose their self-presentational vulnerabilities, including the use of counterfeit products or weight-loss medications. Yet, despite the commonality of such vulnerable self-disclosure, little is known about who discloses, why they do so, and when they choose to reveal or conceal these vulnerabilities. Addressing that gap, we examine how regulatory focus and relationship closeness jointly shape the disclosure of self-presentational vulnerabilities. Across eight studies, we find that prevention-focused (vs. promotion-focused) individuals are more willing to disclose self-presentational vulnerabilities to close others, but not to distant others. We further find that this effect occurs because prevention-focused (vs. promotion-focused) individuals more strongly believe that disclosing such vulnerable information to close others can strengthen their interpersonal relationships.

articles.title: Beliefs About Suffering, Psychological Adjustment, and Prosocial Orientation
articles.authors: Jinyoung Park, Mark R. Leary, Christine Lathren, John M. Davis, Mark Weiser, Rick Hoyle
articles.abstract: People’s beliefs about suffering may shape how they understand and respond to life’s challenges. Across five studies, we tested whether two focal beliefs—that suffering is widely shared/universal and that suffering can be potentially enriching—predict adaptive psychological and prosocial outcomes. College undergraduates who saw their problems as more common reported less distress. U.S. adults who perceived that they experienced a similar amount of suffering as other people and who viewed suffering as enriching demonstrated better adjustment and more adaptive responses to hypothetical challenges. Among Jewish Israeli participants, an enriching view was associated with mental health, common humanity, and support for peaceful resolution of the Israel–Palestine conflict. Finally, reading about suffering as enriching versus depressing increased affective well-being, and framing suffering as universal increased the common-humanity component of compassion. These findings suggest that viewing suffering as universal and potentially enriching supports psychological adjustment and prosocial orientation.

articles.title: The Morality-Effectiveness Disconnect of Pro-Environmental Behaviors
articles.authors: Jareef Martuza, Hege Landsvik
articles.abstract: Not all pro-environmental behaviors are created equal—some are vastly more effective at mitigating climate change than others. Do people judge the more effective behaviors as proportionally more moral? Five main and six supplemental studies ( N = 9,247) across five countries reveal a robust morality-effectiveness disconnect: pro-environmental behaviors that rank better on objective climate-mitigation potential rank worse on individual moral judgments. Laypeople fail to predict this pattern, believing that a positive relationship exists. Furthermore, labeling behaviors by climate impact category reduces the morality-effectiveness disconnect, and detailed impact information reverses it and increases policy endorsement of more effective behaviors over less effective behaviors. While the disconnect primarily stems from effectiveness misperceptions that accurate information can mitigate, we find that personal support for less effective behaviors plays an additional role. Thus, people’s moral intuition for climate action appears miscalibrated: moral cognition can undermine the collective welfare that such cognition should presumably promote.

articles.title: The Pain of Ghosting? People Underestimate How Bad Their Conversation Partners Feel About Not Responding
articles.authors: Sophia Li, Coral Zheng, Juliana Schroeder
articles.abstract: Although online communication platforms provide convenience, they also bring a risk of ghosting , when one person unexpectedly stops responding to another without explanation. Extending prior research that examines the pain of being ghosted, we instead examine whether the act of ghosting itself is emotionally painful – and whether people recognize the extent of ghosters’ bad feelings. Across three studies – recalled real ghosting experiences ( N = 195), imagined ghosting scenarios ( N = 601), and induced ghosting in a live interaction ( N = 350) – we find that people who are ghosted underestimate how bad their conversation partners feel about ghosting them. This underestimation is larger when the ghosting is unintentional and mitigated when communicators do not perceive their actions as ghosting or send a short response (e.g., “sorry, can’t talk”) instead of ghosting. Overall, this research provides a window into the overlooked pain of ghosting others.

articles.title: More Than a Song: Collective Singing Increases Well-being and Self-Expansion Via Collective Effervescence
articles.authors: Shira Gabriel, Nicole Koefler, Michael J. Poulin, Veronica Schneider, Maayan Dvir, Czarina Gutierrez, Esha Naidu
articles.abstract: Humans have been singing with other humans across time and culture. Although past research found positive effects of singing with others, it has not disentangled those effects from being in an established collective. In the current research, we examined the hypothesis that singing in groups leads to increased feelings of well-being and self-expansion even without an established collective. Furthermore, we hypothesized that the main mechanism for these effects is a feeling of collective effervescence—an intertwining sense that one is connected to others and that something special is happening. Finally, we hypothesized that the positive effects of collective effervescence felt during a singing event can last weeks, even months, after the event. Across two experiments and a longitudinal study, we found support for our hypotheses. Singing in groups predicts positive outcomes (e.g., positive mood, satisfaction with life, self-concept change, donation intentions), primarily via the collective effervescence experienced at these events.

articles.title: Diverging Effects of Deliberation: How Perceived Thoughtfulness About Political Issues Affects Character Judgments
articles.authors: Zachary N. Grey, Paul Bloom, Jason E. Plaks, Yoel Inbar
articles.abstract: Across three studies ( N = 896), we examined the effects of perceived deliberation and political (dis)agreement on moral character judgments. We tested whether targets who agree or disagree with the participant on a political issue are evaluated more positively when they are described as deliberating (vs. not deliberating). Results showed that in cases of agreement, there was no effect of deliberation on moral character judgments. This was because deliberators were seen as less certain (which was associated with more negative evaluations) but also more thoughtful (which was associated with more positive evaluations). However, in cases of disagreement, deliberation led to more positive moral character judgments. This was because deliberators were again seen as less certain and more thoughtful, but both perceptions were associated with more positive evaluations. These findings suggest that perceived deliberation makes disagreement more palatable and that people are less concerned with how like-minded people reach their conclusions.

articles.title: Historical Relevance and Modern Perceptions: Mixed-Black and Mixed-Native Racial Categorization and Resource Deservingness
articles.authors: Hailey Shangin, C. Malik Boykin, Tyler Jimenez
articles.abstract: Growing multiracial populations in the United States underscore the evolving complexity of racial identity, particularly in how racial perceptions shape perceived deservingness to resources. This research examines how individuals with Black/White and Native American/White ancestries are categorized and the influence of categorization on perceived deservingness of group-specific resources. It explores the persistence of hypodescent (assigning by non-dominant identity) and hyperdescent (assigning by dominant identity) relating to historical and policy contexts. Across two studies, participants categorized mixed-race targets and evaluated their deservingness for minority-specific resources (i.e., scholarship). Black/White targets were categorized as more Black, consistent with hypodescent bias, while Native/White targets were often categorized as more White, consistent with hyperdescent. Comparatively, these categorizations shaped perceptions of resource deservingness, especially for Black/White targets. This underscores the complexities of perceived multiracial group categorization and may suggest the need for nuanced understanding of racial identity in an increasingly diverse society.

articles.title: Why Poverty in the Present Matters for Intergenerational Concern and the Future of Humanity
articles.authors: Kyle Fiore Law, Stylianos Syropoulos, Amanda Signorini, Christina Jinhee Capozzoli, Liane Young, Brendan Bo O’Connor
articles.abstract: Contrary to perceived tensions between addressing present and future societal needs, we find that present-day poverty and inequality are deeply connected with attitudes toward far-future welfare at both societal and individual levels. Study 1 (144 countries) shows that poorer, more unequal nations score lower on indices of intergenerational concern and farsighted policies. Study 2 (34 countries, N = 123,502) shows that subjective socioeconomic status (SES) predicts greater obligation to sacrifice for future lives, especially in nations with less inequality. In Study 3 ( N = 1,264 Americans), individuals randomly assigned more resources allocate more to future generations, though not proportionately more. Replicating Studies 1 and 2, real-world SES predicts higher donations beyond situational framings. Thus, combatting present-day societal challenges may be key to increasing concern and action for humanity’s future.

articles.title: Action Framing Modulates the Pavlovian Bias in Go and No-Go Learning
articles.authors: Zhang Chen, Senne Braem
articles.abstract: Reward- and punishment-associated (i.e., Pavlovian) cues can trigger specific responses that interfere with learning appropriate actions. Prior work has shown that reward impedes the learning of “no-go” responses, and punishment impedes the learning of “go” responses. This Pavlovian bias is theorized to arise at the motor level and may reflect a rigid coupling between reward and action activation and between punishment and action suppression. Contrary to this view, across two experiments testing adults (one preregistered, total N = 370), using behavioral analyses and computational modeling, we show that action framing strongly modulates Pavlovian bias. When go was framed as approach and no-go as avoidance, we replicated the typical asymmetry in learning. However, when go was framed as avoidance and no-go as approach, this Pavlovian bias disappeared in choice and was attenuated in response times. Pavlovian bias thus operates partly on a semantic level and is more flexible than often theorized.

articles.title: Burnout, Agency, and Postgraduation Plans in Music Student Teachers
articles.authors: Daryl W. Kinney
articles.abstract: Beginning as early as student teaching, teacher burnout has been linked to demography, work conditions, and agency. The purpose of this study was to investigate burnout in music student teachers and how burnout changes during student teaching. Music education majors ( N = 46) enrolled in student teaching at a large Midwestern university in the United States completed the Maslach Burnout Inventory – Educators Survey (MBI-ES) at Weeks 4, 8, and 13 of student teaching, along with surveys measuring agency, postgraduation plans, work/planning hours, and perceptions of support. Repeated-measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) revealed significant effects of agency, postgraduation intentions, and week on MBI-ES burnout dimensions. Higher agency was associated with lower emotional exhaustion and depersonalization and greater personal accomplishment. Those intending to pursue full-time music teaching positions showed lower emotional exhaustion and greater personal accomplishment. Emotional exhaustion decreased from Week 8 to Week 13 among high-agency participants and those planning to teach, yet increased among those with lower agency and no immediate teaching plans. Personal accomplishment increased over time for all participants, remaining higher among those with greater agency and teaching aspirations. Findings highlight the importance of fostering agency and providing targeted support for student teachers, particularly those uncertain about entering the profession.
